common_name: Golden Udo (Sun King, Chartreuse-Leaved Edible-Shoot Ornamental)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Golden Udo, a 2020 Perennial Plant of the Year, is a golden-leaved sport of edible udo bearing brilliant chartreuse-gold foliage best colored in part shade, while still producing edible blanched shoots.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; foliage color is most vivid in a few hours of morning sun with shade during the hottest part of the day, and the leaves turn lime-green rather than scorching in fuller shade. Golden Udo, named the 2020 Perennial Plant of the Year, is a dramatic ornamental sport of the Japanese vegetable udo, producing huge, bold, compound leaves in a luminous chartreuse-gold that light up a shaded border from spring through fall, while retaining the parent species' edible young shoots, which can be blanched and harvested in spring and prepared much like asparagus. It dies back to the ground each winter and re-emerges vigorously in spring, forming a large, architectural clump within a couple of seasons. Divide congested clumps in early spring, and provide consistent moisture, since the large leaves wilt readily in dry soil.

common_name: Sutherland Gold Elderberry (Golden Cutleaf Red Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Sutherland Gold bears finely cut, golden-chartreuse foliage that emerges copper-red, holding up to more sun than most gold-leaved shrubs without scorching, followed by red berries for wildlife.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where the golden foliage color develops best without scorching; it tolerates more sun than most gold-leaved shrubs but still benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates. Sutherland Gold, holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, is a finely dissected, cutleaf selection of red elderberry whose lacy, fern-like leaves emerge coppery-red in spring before maturing to a bright chartreuse-gold that holds color through summer, creating a strikingly textured, glowing accent in the partly shaded border. Clusters of creamy spring flowers are followed by small, bright red berries that ripen in summer, providing food for songbirds, though the raw fruit and other plant parts contain compounds that are toxic to people unless properly cooked. Prune hard in late winter to encourage the largest, most vividly colored new foliage, since the best leaf color and texture appear on vigorous young growth.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Laurel-Leaved Currant is an unusual evergreen currant bearing pendulous, sweetly fragrant greenish-cream flowers in late winter, followed by small edible fruit on pollinated female plants.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to mostly shade or high overhead shade, and shelter from harsh winter wind. Laurel-Leaved Currant is unusual among currants for being evergreen, holding leathery, glossy, laurel-like leaves year-round, and for flowering in the depths of winter, producing hanging clusters of small, sweetly fragrant, greenish-cream flowers from January into March that are a valuable early nectar source for the first bees of the season. Plants are dioecious, so both a male and a female are needed for the female to set its small, edible red-to-black currants, which ripen in early summer and can be used like other currants once fully colored. It is an easy, low-maintenance shrub for the shaded winter garden, valued as much for its fragrance and evergreen structure as for its fruit. Prune only lightly, right after flowering, to remove damaged wood and maintain shape.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Spurless Barrenwort is unusual among Epimedium for bearing spurless, bell-shaped bright-yellow flowers rather than the spurred flowers typical of most species.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; established plants tolerate dry shade well once their roots are settled. Spurless Barrenwort, native to Chinese woodlands, is distinguished from most other Epimedium species by its flowers, which lack the characteristic backward-pointing spurs and instead open as simple, dangling, bright golden-yellow bells held above the wiry stems in spring, a notably different flower form from the spurred, often bicolor blooms typical of the genus. The heart-shaped leaflets, often bronze-tinted when young, form an attractive, semi-evergreen groundcover mat that spreads slowly by rhizomes. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge, to fully display the blooms, and divide congested clumps in early spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Pink Young's Barrenwort (Roseum, Nodding Pink Bishop's Hat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Roseum bears nodding, purplish-pink flowers, a distinct color from the white-flowered 'Niveum' form of the same hybrid already common in gardens.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Roseum is a classic, long-cultivated cultivar of Young's Barrenwort bearing dainty, nodding, purplish-pink flowers with paler spurs in mid-spring, held just above neat, compact mounds of heart-shaped leaflets that emerge bronze-tinted before turning green, a soft pastel color option alongside the white-flowered 'Niveum' form of the same hybrid. Its compact, dense habit makes it well suited to the front of a shaded border or as a small-scale groundcover beneath shrubs and trees. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to fully display the blooms, and divide congested clumps in early spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Dwarf Yellow Toad Lily (Low Stoloniferous Unspotted Yellow Tricyrtis)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in mostly to full shade; Dwarf Yellow Toad Lily bears clear, unspotted bright yellow flowers on a low, stoloniferous clump, distinct from the white or purple-spotted flowers typical of most toad lilies.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in mostly to full shade. Dwarf Yellow Toad Lily, native to Japan, is unusual within its genus for bearing clear, unspotted, bright golden-yellow, star-shaped flowers in late summer and fall, a striking departure from the white or purple-spotted blooms typical of the more commonly grown toad lilies, held on a low, spreading clump that increases by creeping stolons to form a modest groundcover over time. Its compact stature suits the front of a shaded border or a woodland rock garden better than the taller upright toad lily species. Keep soil evenly moist, since it does not tolerate drought well, and divide congested patches in spring to control spread or increase plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Chocoholic bears bronze-purple foliage and mauve-pink bottlebrush flowers that fade to white, a distinct bloom color from the white-flowered dark-leaved bugbane cultivars already common in cultivation.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, deep, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Chocoholic, a seedling selection of the popular dark-leaved 'Brunette', bears the same rich bronze-purple, deeply cut foliage but is distinguished by its flower color, opening mauve-pink rather than pure white and gradually fading toward white as the tall, fragrant bottlebrush spikes age in late summer and early fall, a subtle but distinctive departure from other dark bugbane cultivars. The dark foliage glows in dappled shade and provides months of textural contrast against nearby hostas and ferns before the late-season flower spikes extend the display well past when most shade perennials have finished blooming. Performs best in cooler climates; in the warmth of zone 8, provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture. Divide in spring only when necessary, since established clumps resent disturbance.

common_name: Aurora Fernleaf Bleeding Heart (White-Flowered Summer-Persistent Dicentra)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Aurora bears pure white flowers over blue-green ferny foliage and, kept moist, stays in active growth through summer rather than going dormant like common bleeding heart.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, spacing 12 to 18 inches apart. Aurora bears pure white, dangling, heart-shaped flowers held above finely dissected, blue-green ferny foliage, a clean white counterpart to the pink-flowered wild form of Western Bleeding Heart, and if kept consistently moist through summer it remains in active growth and continues flowering intermittently rather than going summer-dormant the way common bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis) does. It spreads gently by rhizomes and self-sowing to form an attractive groundcover colony in cool, moist, shaded sites, working well under conifers and deciduous trees alongside ferns and other woodland perennials. In hot climates it may still go dormant in summer heat but reliably re-emerges in fall or the following spring. Divide in early spring to increase plantings.

common_name: Betberg Solomon's Seal (Bronze-Emerging Spring Foliage Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Betberg emerges deep bronze-purple in spring before greening up, a foliage-color trait distinct from the plain-green and variegated Solomon's Seal cultivars already common in cultivation.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade, though it performs best and lasts longest in partial to full shade in warm climates. Betberg is prized for its striking spring emergence, when the arching stems and paired leaves unfurl a deep, glossy bronze-purple before gradually shifting to the typical fresh green through late spring, a distinctive seasonal color display not seen in the plain-green or white-edged Solomon's Seal cultivars more commonly grown. Small, dangling, white, bell-shaped flowers hang in pairs from the leaf axils in late spring, followed by blue-black berries in fall. It is an easy, long-lived, essentially carefree woodland perennial, spreading slowly by rhizomes to form an increasingly graceful colony, and combines beautifully with ferns, hostas, and hellebores. Cut stems back to the ground after they yellow in fall.

common_name: Chinese Sweet Box (Compact Fragrant Winter-Flowering Sarcococca)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Chinese Sweet Box, native to Jiangxi, China, is a distinct Sarcococca species from the more commonly grown S. hookeriana, forming a compact, rounded mound of glossy evergreen foliage with fragrant midwinter flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it performs best in low light and can struggle in strong sun. Chinese Sweet Box, native to Jiangxi Province, China, and genuinely distinct from the widely planted Sarcococca hookeriana, forms a compact, rounded mound of glossy, deep-green, evergreen foliage that provides reliable year-round structure in the shaded garden, producing small, inconspicuous but powerfully sweet-scented white flowers in the depths of winter that perfume the surrounding air, followed by small black berries. Its dense, tidy habit and shade tolerance make it a valuable evergreen filler beneath trees, along shaded foundations, or as a low informal hedge where winter fragrance near a path or entry is wanted. Water during dry spells and prune lightly after flowering only if needed to maintain shape; otherwise it requires very little maintenance.

common_name: Codsall Pink Deutzia (Fully Double Pink-Flushed Rough Deutzia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Codsall Pink bears fully double, pink-flushed flowers, unlike the single-flowered species and the white 'Pride of Rochester' already common in cultivation.

directions: Root cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; deutzia blooms on old wood and should be pruned right after flowering by thinning the oldest, flowered stems to the ground to maintain vigor and density. Codsall Pink bears fully double flowers, each with an extra ruffle of petals flushed rose-pink on the outer surface and paler within, in dense, upright panicles covering the arching branches in late spring and early summer, a richer, showier bloom than the single white flowers of the species or the semi-double 'Pride of Rochester'. It tolerates partial shade acceptably and, like other deutzias, develops attractive exfoliating warm-brown bark on older stems that adds winter interest once the leaves have dropped. An easy, trouble-free, long-lived deciduous shrub for the mixed border.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Rosea is a historic 1906 cultivar with salmon-pink flower spikes, distinct from the white-flowered 'Sixteen Candles' and the deeper pink 'Ruby Spice' already common in cultivation.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; summersweet tolerates shade well and is commonly used as understory planting beneath larger trees, though it flowers most heavily with a few hours of morning sun. Rosea, introduced in 1906 and one of the oldest named summersweet cultivars still in cultivation, bears dense, upright spikes of fragrant, soft salmon-pink flowers in midsummer, buds opening a deeper rose-pink that fades gently as they age, a distinct, historic color option from the pure white 'Sixteen Candles' and 'September Beauty' and the deeper 'Ruby Spice' selected decades later. Its intensely sweet, spicy fragrance perfumes the garden for weeks and draws heavy pollinator traffic from bees and butterflies. It tolerates wet soil better than most shrubs, making it useful along ponds or low spots, and suckers gently over time to form a colony. Prune immediately after flowering if size control is needed.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Camouflage bears large palmate leaves splashed chartreuse-to-gold in a dappled-light pattern, distinct from plain-green Fatsia japonica and the white-edged 'Spider's Web'.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from harsh wind and hot midday sun, which can scorch the variegated leaf patches. Camouflage bears the same bold, glossy, deeply lobed palmate leaves that make Fatsia japonica a dramatic architectural shade shrub, but each leaf is irregularly splashed with chartreuse to gold blotches in a mottled, dappled-light pattern reminiscent of sun flecks on a forest floor, a distinct variegation style from the plain green species or the crisp white margins of 'Spider's Web'. Small, rounded clusters of white flowers appear in fall on mature plants, followed by black berries. It is an excellent large-leaved accent for a shaded courtyard or foundation planting, bringing bold tropical texture and color to deep shade where few other shrubs perform as well. Water during dry spells and prune only to remove damaged or overly long stems.
